title_en: What markets make of the midterms
Lula’s victory in the 2026 Brazilian elections was far from inevitable
excerpt_en: First round result was a warning against complacency, but the runoof comeback does not resolve the structural tensions facing a fourth Lula administration.
body_en: On 25 October 2026, Brazil’s President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva secured a fourth term in an election that exposed both the resilience of Brazilian democracy and the depth of the far right’s social roots. Lula received 51.79% of valid votes in the runoff against far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro’s 48.21%.

Three weeks earlier, however, the outcome had looked very different: Flávio - son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, now jailed for a coup attempt after losing his bid for reelection in 2022 - led the first round with 47.03% of the valid votes, compared with Lula’s 45.16%. The reversal was not simply an electoral comeback. It revealed how a campaign that had failed to generate enthusiasm could be transformed through collective mobilization, both online and in the streets.

The first round result was a warning against complacency. Lula’s campaign leaned heavily on his historical achievements and the restoration of policies associated with his previous Workers’ Party (PT) governments. These accomplishments were real, but they did not necessarily offer a persuasive answer to a question increasingly heard among voters: what comes next?

For those who have voted for Lula repeatedly over decades, the promise of continuity could coexist with political fatigue. His age and the campaign’s difficulty in speaking to younger voters added to this sense of exhaustion. Meanwhile, the assumption that Jair Bolsonaro’s imprisonment had removed any serious electoral threat proved dangerously mistaken.

A central contradiction was that the defense of social policies did not automatically translate into a sense of economic security. Many households continued to experience the erosion of purchasing power, high borrowing costs and persistent indebtedness. According to a Brazil’s National Confederation of Commerce’s July 2026 survey, 82% of Brazilian families reported outstanding debts, 29.8% had overdue bills, and debt payments absorbed approximately 29.5% of monthly household income. Among families earning up to three times the country’s minimum wage, indebtedness reached 84.9%.

The politics of everyday insecurity Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign managed to combine continuity and novelty. His surname preserved his father’s political identity and loyal electorate, while his comparatively younger image, disciplined media performances and lack of experience in the federal Executive allowed him to present himself as an alternative to incumbent Lula.
Flávio was not a political outsider: his legislative career was substantial. Yet the campaign’s effectiveness lay in its ability to turn familiar grievances into an apparently new political offer.

Public security was especially important in this. Fear of street crime, mobile phone theft and drug trafficking were connected to a broader discourse of order and punishment. The invocation of “narcoterrorism” also resonated with the language of United States’ President Donald Trump administration, demonstrating how domestic electoral agendas are increasingly entangled with geopolitical narratives. The campaign likewise foregrounded supermarket prices, debt and the difficulty saving money. Not every issue was directly within the federal government’s remit, but the political effect was to hold Lula accountable for the totality of everyday insecurity.

The territorial pattern of the vote also matters. The first round strength of the far right in rural regions and municipalities in the country’s interior points to the consolidation of what might be called agribusiness linked “Bolsonarismo”. This is not to suggest that agribusiness is politically homogeneous, or that every rural voter supports the far right.

Rather, it indicates that a powerful political alignment has taken shape across parts of Brazil’s Center-West, the interior of populous and rich São Paulo state and other areas where export oriented agriculture exercises economic and social influence. Its expansion into new agricultural frontiers, including the “MATOPIBA” region - encompassing parts of Maranhão, Tocantins, Piauí and Bahia states, between the Center-West and Northeast regions of the country - merits systematic electoral and territorial research.

“From mourning to struggle” The morning after the first round of the election on October 4 was marked by a profound sense of defeat in Lula’s campaign. Flávio had finished ahead, and the far right had strengthened its institutional presence. The possibility of a return to Bolsonarismo was no longer abstract. Yet, mourning quickly gave way to mobilization. In Portuguese, the transition can be captured in a phrase that is difficult to translate without losing its force: “do luto à luta”, or “from mourning to struggle”.

Students took to the streets in Rio de Janeiro state; and soon after marches and smaller neighborhood actions multiplied. Artists, musicians, trade unions and people with little previous experience of organized politics joined demonstrations, leafleting, cultural events and local conversations.

It was not merely a sequence of large political rallies. Its significance lay in the diffusion of political activity into everyday spaces: campuses, homes, cultural centers, workplaces and neighborhood networks. Lula’s campaign gained more capillarity, extending beyond the formal structures of parties and electoral committees.

Digital mobilization developed in parallel. Influencers urged supporters to remain active, and a WhatsApp channel created by Brazilian congressman André Janones - “Lula’s Army” - provided a recognizable language for coordinated social media campaigning. Supporters exchanged practical guidance about posting, sharing and the unintended consequences of amplifying adversarial content. The far right had long invested in these techniques. What was striking in the runoff was the left’s rapid appropriation of similar forms of distributed communication.

But the most important innovation was not technological. It was political. Online networks and street mobilization reinforced one another. Digital messages brought people into public spaces, while visible demonstrations gave online activism a sense of momentum and legitimacy. In a fragmented media environment, neither the street nor the screen was sufficient on its own.

title_en: Elon Musk’s nearly half a billion dollars in midterms spending was a flop
excerpt_en: The tech billionaire set spending record as he poured $446m into campaigns for failed Republican candidates
body_en: Elon Musk set a record for election spending this year after pouring nearly half a billion dollars into backing Republicans in the US midterm elections. It turned out to be a poor investment.

The SpaceX and Tesla CEO contributed at least $446m to Republican-aligned Super Pacs and groups over the course of the elections, specifically targeting several key Senate races in an effort to help the Trump administration retain Republican control of Congress. He outdid his own 2024 spending of nearly $290m. Yet as Democrats swept to power across the country on Tuesday night, it became clear that Musk would get nearly nothing in return for his hundreds of millions in spending.

Democrats won every one of the five Senate races where Musk’s America Pac spent the most money backing Republican candidates. In Texas, where Musk’s empire is based and where he directed most of his political efforts, Republicans lost the Senate race, governor’s office and are expected to relinquish control of the state house.
Related: The staggering $446m Elon Musk has spent on the US midterms – visualized

After months of Musk posting attacks on Democrats and amplifying election conspiracy theories on X, the tech mogul was unusually quiet on election night. He jokingly posted “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” but the top Republican mega-donor was otherwise largely silent on the results.

Musk’s losses from midterms go beyond the enormous sums that he dumped into failed campaigns, however, potentially ending an era of lax regulation and cozy relations with state officials that has benefitted his companies. The world’s richest person will soon face a House, Senate and Texas government filled with Democrats that have vowed to take a tougher stance on tech and specifically scrutinize his operations in particular.

Altogether, Musk’s political spending this midterms flowed into at least eight Republican-aligned Super Pacs that targeted races across the country, with the largest donation of at least $216m going into his own America Pac. He also gave $168m to the Senate Leadership Fund, which backed a series of candidates that included the Texas Republican Ken Paxton.

Out of all of Musk’s political activity in midterms, the contest where he put the most money and focus was the Senate race in Texas between Paxton and Democrat James Talarico. America Pac spent at least $28m on anti-Talarico ad buys and messaging alone, while Musk repeatedly posted attacks on X, his social media platform, such as “Talarico wants to trans your kids and destroy the border.”
After Talarico achieved a commanding win on Tuesday night, the Democratic senator-elect referenced Musk in his victory speech.
“We just proved that all the money in the world is no match for the people of Texas,” Talarico said. “We just sent a message to every billionaire mega-donor, every trillionaire mega-donor.”

Senate races in Michigan, Maine, Ohio and Iowa similarly went for Democratic candidates after America Pac spent tens of millions supporting Republican campaigns. The Pac’s money had gone into attack ads that focused on transgender rights or accused Democrats of being radical socialists.
Related: Trump’s billionaire-blue collar coalition has been smashed by class politics | Aditya Chakrabortty

Even if Musk’s spending was not successful, it doesn’t mean it wasn’t impactful. Musk and the Super Pacs’ expenditures created several of the most expensive races in US history and set a potential precedent for how much spending will take place in the 2028 presidential election. It will also probably spur months of analysis around the limits of what money can buy in politics.

Musk’s businesses have benefitted greatly from lucrative contracts with the Trump administration, as well as Trump’s hands-off approach to regulating artificial intelligence. In Texas, the state legislature and Governor Greg Abbott have provided him a friendly environment to do business while passing laws backed by the billionaire’s lobbyists.

Gina Hinojosa, the incoming Democratic governor in Texas,will probably take a more critical stance towards Musk and his businesses. Hinojosa has called for a datacenter moratorium and has been in a legal battle in recent months to gain access to unredacted emails between Abbott’s office and Musk. Meanwhile, House Democrats have called for launching investigations into Musk’s conduct while he was leader of the so-called “department of government efficiency” last year and vowed to scrutinize federal funding for his companies.

title_en: UK and Caribbean to begin ‘dialogue’ within next year after slavery reparations call
excerpt_en: Antigua and Barbuda’s prime minister says there was a consensus at Commonwealth summit on way forward
body_en: The UK has agreed to “structured dialogue” in the next year with Caribbean nations affected by the slave trade and its legacy, Commonwealth leaders have said.

Gaston Browne, Antigua and Barbuda’s prime minister, said there was a “consensus” in discussions between governments about a way forward on slavery reparations at the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm).
“There’s camaraderie and where we have issues that potentially could have divided us, we’re able to come to a consensus on the way forward,” he said.
Browne also praised UK prime minister Andy Burnham for being “very assertive in addressing [the] issue”.

“Perhaps there are some who believe that he may have dodged the issue as a relatively new prime minister. I think he has shown a significant amount of courage and goodwill, and I can tell you that he has developed a lot of goodwill with the Caribbean nations.

“And this structured dialogue that he has proposed, we are hoping that it will take place sometime within the next 12 months. We have also agreed in principle that by the end of this year, or early next year, that the whole framework for the dialogue would be established.”
Browne said the region would not be making “unreasonable demands on the United Kingdom”.
Burnham announced on Friday that he wanted to begin a structured dialogue and was open to Britain apologising, but ruled out reparations.
Instead, he proposed discussions on debt resets for smaller Commonwealth nations and announced £40m ($54m) for critical infrastructure in the Caribbean over the next three years.

A 10-point plan drawn up by the Caribbean Community’s reparations commission, which outlines the region’s vision for reparations, specifically asks for “debt cancellation” – not debt restructuring – and “monetary compensation”, arguing that former colonies’ “existing debts are intergenerational and are ultimately and intimately tied to centuries of colonial extraction”.

Asked whether Caribbean nations would urge Burnham to approach the talks with an open mind on reparations, Browne said: “We see the prime minister as an open-minded person, and the issue certainly will be raised.

“On the commencement of the structured dialogue, he has taken his position and we are very clear on our position that reparations are important, that reparations must be part of this structured dialogue and we remain very optimistic that we will come to a consensus on the issue.”
Leading figures in the Caribbean reparatory justice movement have said that debt relief and development assistance from the UK cannot be a replacement for reparations for centuries of slavery.

Ralph Gonsalves, a former prime minister of St Vincent and the Grenadines and a senior figure in the reparatory justice movement’s Repair Campaign, said: “When I listened to Andy Burnham, and I listened to the king, and they’re talking about what is helpful is not reparations, but for them to work on specific things like debt relief, and education and health, and climate change infrastructure.
“Now, all those things are within the 10-point plan. But they are also within the sustainable development goals of 2015, which we all signed on to at the United Nations,” he told the Guardian.

He added: “There are things in the reparatory justice 10-point plan which deal with issues … the first one is the ecology, and then psychological repair. And for people like members of the Rastafari faith, or brothers and sisters who may wish repatriation, that’s something we have to work out with African countries, those who want to go back. But there are financial implications in that. So you’ll have to have a separate carve-out on the basis of the 10-point plan.”
Labour MP Bell Ribeiro-Addy, chair of the House of Commons’ all-party parliamentary group for Afrikan Reparations, said the question was fundamentally about “agency”.

Speaking at an event on Tuesday to launch a “ global reparations caravan ”, which will travel across countries to educate and engage people in the reparations movement, she said: “So when it comes now to reparative justice, and as we move forward in the movement, I have to be clear with everybody, it has to be about agency, not making deals here and there, because agency was the crime. When you think about what was taken from people of African descent when they were enslaved, it was their agency, their right to decide all of these different things about their lives.

“So when reparative justice arrangements are being made, it absolutely has to be made with those who were affected, because if it is done to us, it is not reparations. I don’t know what it is, but it is not reparative justice.”

Gonsalves said the danger of reducing reparatory justice to development assistance was that such assistance remained discretionary on the UK’s part. “We have to understand the specificities of reparatory justice as distinct from general sustainable development goals. They’re shaping the discussion only within the frame of sustainable development goals,” he said.
Related: King Charles addresses summit as demands for slavery apology grow

Prof Kingsley Abbott, a human rights lawyer and director of the Institute of Commonwealth Studies at the University of London, also stressed the importance of harmed communities having a decisive say in what reparations should entail.

title_en: Swapping from dairy to plant-based milk, cheese and yoghurt ‘could lead to micronutrient deficiencies’
excerpt_en: Young people and women most at risk, study finds, as researchers call for vegan products to be fortified with iodine in particular
body_en: Switching from dairy products to plant-based alternatives could lead to deficiencies in vital micronutrients, especially among young people and women, a study has found.

Even moving partly to vegan alternatives to milk, cheese and yoghurt could lead to falls in iodine, calcium, riboflavin and vitamin B12 if the substitutes, often based on soya, almonds or oats, are not fortified, scientists said.

The greatest concerns surround iodine, a trace element used by the thyroid gland to produce hormones that regulate metabolism and support healthy growth and brain development. More than half of UK teenage girls already have inadequate iodine intake, the researchers said.

Replacing a fifth to a third of dairy intake with plant-based alternatives would lead to prevalence of iodine deficiency rising from 54% to 65% of adolescent girls and from 32% to 42% of women aged 19 to 49 years old, according to modelling based on typical market levels of fortification.

“There are known health effects of iodine deficiency and that’s why we want to raise awareness of this,” said Dr Sarah Bath, an associate professor in public health nutrition at the University of Surrey. “The population groups that seem to be at risk and have the lowest intakes were the young women and women of childbearing age, and that’s the key life stage where iodine is particularly important.”
Plant-based alternatives to milk, cheese and yoghurt have grown in popularity, though there are signs some consumers are shifting back.

In the UK, children get about half, and adults about a third, of their total iodine intake from dairy products, but there is no formal requirement for vegan alternatives to be fortified with micronutrients.

The researchers looked at the impact of replacing dairy with plant-based alternatives on the UK market, including 146 non-dairy milks, 76 yoghurts and 67 cheeses. While 61% had added calcium and 46% added vitamin B12, only 19% were fortified with riboflavin and 12% with iodine.

At these levels, the scientists’ modelling showed that swapping a third of dairy intake for vegan alternatives led to a 9% to 21% drop in iodine intake, with calcium, riboflavin and vitamin B12 also falling. Switching to 100% non-dairy alternatives led to inadequate levels of iodine reaching 80% in teenage girls and 72% in teenage boys.

Requiring all non-dairy alternatives to be fortified with iodine would prevent average declines, the study found. Adding iodised salt to bread helped reduce the proportion of teenage girls with inadequate iodine intake in the modelled scenarios. The study is published in the Lancet Planetary Health.

Some companies already fortify their dairy substitutes. Niamh Brannelly, the head of nutrition and science communications for Danone in the UK, said its core range of Alpro products was fortified for calcium, iodine and vitamins B2 and B12.

Caroline Orfila Jenkins, a vice-president for science and technology at Oatly, said all its unflavoured, non-organic oat drinks were fortified with nutrients including iodine, calcium, riboflavin and vitamins B12 and D. “This research underlines the importance of appropriate fortification as diets become more plant-based,” she said.

Nichola Ludlam-Raine, a registered dietitian and spokesperson for the British Dietetic Association, said the work raised an important population-level concern but did not mean that everyone who switched would become nutrient-deficient because overall diet mattered too.

“For anyone choosing plant-based milk, I’d recommend checking the label and choosing one fortified with iodine, such as Alpro,” she said. “Organic drinks aren’t fortified with added nutrients, so they’re unlikely to provide iodine. White fish such as cod or haddock, as well as eggs and yoghurt and kefir for those who consume them, can also contribute iodine. I wouldn’t recommend relying on seaweed or kelp supplements as an iodine source, as the iodine content can vary widely and may be excessive.”

title_en: Vermont Was Supposed to Get an Audit of Its Lake Champlain Cleanup. It Never Happened.
excerpt_en: The post Vermont Was Supposed to Get an Audit of Its Lake Champlain Cleanup. It Never Happened. appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: Cyanobacteria blooms in a tributary of Lake Champlain in the town of St. Albans, Vermont, in August. Caleb Kenna for ProPublica This summer, Vermont’s Clean Water Board celebrated a milestone: Over the past decade, the state has invested nearly a billion dollars to clean up its polluted streams, rivers and lakes. The vast majority of that money has gone toward Lake Champlain.
“I think that’s something to be extremely proud of,” said Douglas Farnham, the board’s chair.
Vermont was supposed to get an independent evaluation of what it has gotten for all that money. But that study was never done.

A decade ago, Vermont lawmakers mandated that the board submit an audit from an outside environmental consultant to determine whether the projects the state had invested in to improve water quality were working. The audit also was meant to examine whether the state’s agriculture and natural resource agencies are doing enough to enforce water quality regulations on farms, which are the biggest source of phosphorus in Lake Champlain.

Do You Live Near Lake Champlain? Help Seven Days and ProPublica Investigate Algae Blooms. Seven Days and ProPublica have teamed up to investigate the cleanup of Lake Champlain. Have you been affected by this issue? We’d like to hear from you.

Get In Touch Lake Champlain has been overloaded with phosphorus-laden runoff from farms, roads and urban sewers for decades. That pollution fuels potentially toxic blue-green algae blooms that have raised health concerns and hurt the state’s tourism industry. Under sustained pressure from citizens, environmental advocates and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, Vermont’s leaders embarked on an ambitious initiative to improve the lake’s water quality, enshrined in the state’s landmark 2015 Clean Water Act.

Now, halfway through a 20-year cleanup effort mandated by the EPA, some lawmakers worry they don’t have enough information to ensure that the state is pursuing the most cost-effective cleanup strategies.

When lawmakers approved the clean water law, they took the major step of establishing a fund to pay for the cleanup and a board to administer it. Since 2016, Vermont has disbursed $928 million — $755 million in state funding and $173 million in local and federal dollars — on water quality projects and programs. That’s nearly as much as what Vermont has spent on paving and resurfacing state highways over the past decade.
As part of the law, the legislature also required the board’s leaders to provide it with a full program audit by January 2021.
But the board received no responses to an initial request for proposals in 2020. Lawmakers extended the deadline to 2023. Yet again, no outside firms bid on the audit.

Farnham said the board received informal feedback from some firms that the audit’s scope was too broad and complex. He reported back to fellow board members that he and Julie Moore, secretary of the Vermont Agency of Natural Resources, had asked legislators what to do next but didn’t receive any clear suggestions.
The board never issued a new request or revisited the matter (until Seven Days and ProPublica recently asked about it), and Vermont’s legislature never followed up to narrow the scope.

Water with particles of cyanobacteria, collected in mid-August from Lake Champlain in St. Albans Lake Champlain Committee monitor Jon Twombly, courtesy of Lake Champlain Committee St. Albans in late August during a high-alert bloom day Volunteer photo courtesy of Vermont Department of Health Former state Rep. David Deen, who sponsored the clean water law and retired in 2018, said he was dismayed to learn that the audit never happened.
“Personally, I find it amazing that they haven’t done that audit and that somebody in the legislature did not hold them to account to conduct that audit,” he said.

Rep. Amy Sheldon, the longtime chair of the House Committee on Environment, recalled hearing about the audit challenges but noted that it’s difficult for the legislature to follow up because Vermont’s lawmakers don’t have staff. In the other chamber, former state Sen. Chris Bray, who chaired the natural resources committee until 2025, said he did not recall hearing about the missing audit.

In an interview, Farnham acknowledged that an outside audit would be helpful. But he said the board already has robust tools for assessing progress through a yearly performance report compiled by the Vermont Department of Environmental Conservation, which coordinates and tracks most of the state’s clean water spending.
“We’ve got enough eyes coming at it from different angles that I think that mutes the need for that comprehensive audit,” he said.

The annual reporting process has improved greatly since the audit was mandated, and the DEC’s website “provides a lot of transparency,” about how the state is spending clean water money and the results, said Emily Bird, director of the department’s Water Investment Division.

But some current and former state officials say that approach isn’t a substitute for an audit to determine whether Vermont is getting adequate and cost-effective returns on its huge water quality investments.

The last independent assessment of clean water spending was a 2019 report from the state auditor. It found that a disproportionate amount of money was being spent on wastewater treatment plants, which contributed by far the smallest share of phosphorus pollution, instead of targeting bigger sources such as agriculture.

That mismatch persists seven years later. Agriculture is the largest source of phosphorus runoff, yet agricultural water quality programs receive less than a third of the total clean water funding in the current budget.

title_en: Vermont Has Spent Nearly a Billion Dollars to Clean Up Lake Champlain. But the Green Slime Keeps Coming Back.
excerpt_en: The post Vermont Has Spent Nearly a Billion Dollars to Clean Up Lake Champlain. But the Green Slime Keeps Coming Back. appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: Jeff van den Noort collects a sample outside his home in North Hero, Vermont, for the Lake Champlain Committee’s cyanobacteria monitoring program. Caleb Kenna for ProPublica On the last day of August, Jeff van den Noort spotted thick swirls of neon green film coating the water just steps from his home in Vermont. He waded in up to his ankles and dipped a jar to get a sample of the scum.

It wasn’t the first time he’d seen the slime. Since his parents bought the house on an island in Lake Champlain in 1966, van den Noort has spent part of nearly every summer in this quiet spot. Back then, the lake was clear.

But he began to witness the water’s deterioration as he grew older, especially after he moved into the home full time in 2010 to care for his ailing mother. That day in late August was the worst he’d seen all summer.

Later that week, van den Noort grabbed a bucket, a few Mason jars and a smartphone and got into his rusty Saab. He drove past the boat launches, frozen-in-time general stores and windswept pastures of the lake’s islands in northern Vermont and stopped at four other spots along the shore. Each time, he collected some murky water, gauged how thick the muck was, took a few photos and jotted down the weather conditions. He then uploaded his report to an online database.

Van den Noort was one part of a large volunteer effort to monitor a problem that has plagued Lake Champlain, which supplies drinking water to about 200,000 people. In recent decades, blooms of potentially toxic cyanobacteria, often called blue-green algae, have killed pets, forced beaches to close and hurt business and property values along the shores of this iconic Vermont feature.
“I just don’t feel like enough is being done,” van den Noort said. “And I think the state needs to take this seriously.”

A cyanobacteria bloom mixes with duckweed on the shoreline of Lake Champlain in the town of St. Albans, Vermont, in early August. Courtesy of Lake Champlain Committee Just over a decade ago, state leaders seemed to be doing just that. In 2015, then-Gov. Peter Shumlin stood a few feet from Lake Champlain by the Burlington waterfront and signed Vermont’s Clean Water Act. It promised to tighten limits on pollution and provide funding to clean up the state’s waterways.

The move was a response to ratcheting pressure from environmentalists and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. The EPA had been telling Vermont officials for years that they needed to take much stronger action. In 2016, the agency finalized tougher cleanup targets that the state must meet by 2036.

But after 10 years and nearly a billion dollars spent on water quality projects and programs, Vermont’s cleanup effort is faltering. In a little-noticed letter to the head of Vermont’s Department of Environmental Conservation last year, the EPA’s regional administrator warned that the state was “not on track” to meet its cleanup goal and would need to more than double its annual pace.

Halfway through the two-decade timetable, Vermont has achieved only 35% of the goal, according to the state’s most recent estimates. And the steps that Vermont has taken to get there, such as upgrading sewage treatment plants, represent “low-hanging fruit,” Eric Perkins, a former EPA official involved in setting the target, wrote in an email in response to questions from Seven Days and ProPublica.

The culprit behind these blooms is phosphorus, an element that is an essential building block of life, present in all organic matter. But too much of it has been pouring into the lake from farm fields saturated with fertilizer and manure, dirty stormwater, and raw sewage from treatment plants overwhelmed by heavy rains. That has tipped the lake’s ecosystem out of balance, spurring the growth of microorganisms that turn shallow bays and shorelines into no-go zones.

Ingesting cyanobacteria-laden water can cause vomiting, diarrhea, dizziness and liver damage, while skin contact can lead to rashes. Researchers have also detected possible links between chronic exposure to cyanobacteria and heightened risk of Parkinson’s disease and ALS, also known as Lou Gehrig’s disease. The algae blooms can also deprive fish and other aquatic life of oxygen.

While some areas of Lake Champlain have seen incremental improvements in phosphorus concentrations and cyanobacteria blooms, other parts of the lake are getting worse. Seven of the lake’s 15 sampling stations have exceeded the EPA’s annual phosphorus limits every year since 2015, a Seven Days and ProPublica analysis of lake monitoring data through 2025 shows. Four stations recorded higher average phosphorus levels over the past decade than in the decade before, including in the southern part of the lake and its northeast arm.

People enjoy the water at North Beach on Lake Champlain in Burlington, Vermont, on Labor Day weekend. Algae blooms sometimes force the city to close the beach. Caleb Kenna for ProPublica In September, the Department of Environmental Conservation reported to the EPA that in two northeastern sections of the lake most chronically plagued by phosphorus runoff, the state is not nearly on track to meet its targets. The department specifically acknowledged that it was not making enough progress in addressing stormwater runoff and that reductions in farm pollution in the Missisquoi River watershed have slowed since 2023.

Vermont shares the 120-mile-long lake with New York and Quebec, but it’s the source of about two-thirds of the phosphorus that flows into the water body. Agriculture is the largest polluting sector, while stormwater runoff from development, like urban parking lots and rural roads, contributes the highest amount of phosphorus per acre.

title_en: Do You Live Near Lake Champlain? Help Seven Days and ProPublica Investigate Algae Blooms.
excerpt_en: The post Do You Live Near Lake Champlain? Help Seven Days and ProPublica Investigate Algae Blooms. appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: People enjoying the water at North Beach on Lake Champlain in Burlington, Vermont. The beach occasionally gets closed because of algae blooms. Caleb Kenna for ProPublica Despite being an iconic part of Vermont’s landscape and a large source of the state’s drinking water, Lake Champlain has been polluted for decades. Phosphorus runoff from farm fields, rural roads, parking lots, stormwater drains and wastewater treatment plants flows into the lake, fueling algae blooms that frequently choke its bays and shorelines.

Vermont is halfway through a 20-year effort to clean up the lake. In 2016, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency established new, stricter requirements for reducing phosphorus runoff that the state must meet by 2036. But more than a decade in, after spending nearly a billion dollars, the state is lagging behind. Water quality has not improved dramatically, and in some parts of the lake, it is getting worse. This past summer algae blooms shut down swimming at public beaches in St. Albans Bay in the northeast part of the lake.

Seven Days and ProPublica have teamed up to understand the reasons behind this lack of progress. We want to know how pollution in the lake is affecting Vermont’s economy and the lifestyles and livelihoods of Vermonters and visitors alike. We’re also interested in learning more about how persistently poor water quality in Lake Champlain affects Vermonters’ health, well-being and finances.

Do you live, play or depend on Lake Champlain? We want to hear from you. Your perspective will help us understand how longstanding pollution affects a wide range of issues, from drinking water quality to tax revenue from tourism around the lake.

We’re gathering these stories for our reporting, which can take several weeks or months. We may not be able to follow up with everyone, but we will read everything you submit and it will help guide our project.

title_en: David Jones goes into administration, with store closures expected and thousands of jobs at risk
excerpt_en: Future of department store in jeopardy after years of steep losses, with outer suburban and regional locations vulnerable
body_en: Australia’s premier upmarket department store David Jones has collapsed into voluntary administration, putting thousands of jobs at risk and leaving the future of the 188-year-old retailer hanging in the balance.

The upheaval follows years of steep losses and underperforming stores that left the heritage retailer falling behind on rent, culminating in a breakdown of negotiations with its primary landlord, Westfield owner Scentre Group.

Staff were informed on Thursday that the David Jones board had appointed voluntary administrators from McGrathNicol, before the retailer’s main financier promptly installed FTI Consulting as receivers.
Related: David Jones held many rites of passage for Australians. Lately it feels like death by a thousand cuts | Glynis Traill-Nash
Under the dual appointment, FTI will take day-to-day control of operations, running the department store network while it restructures the business.
The process will almost certainly trigger immediate store closures, though receivers will try keep the core network open while hunting for fresh capital.
Analysts expect closures to hit outer-suburban and regional mall locations hardest, likely sparing premier CBD flagship stores.
Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email David Jones employs more than 6,000 staff across a network of 38 stores.
Creditors are scheduled to meet next week, according to the Shop, Distributive and Allied Employees’ Association.
The national secretary of the SDA, Gerard Dwyer, told the ABC the top priority was to retain as many jobs as possible.
“We do not want to see the end of David Jones, so perhaps it is a smaller model that then rebuilds and goes from there,” Dwyer said.
“Smaller is better than no David Jones, and a smaller David Jones can then deal with some of the challenges that they’ve obviously been facing.”

The administration could leave unsecured creditors with substantial losses, with unpaid product suppliers, some of which had already begun redirecting stock to their own retail outlets, and shoppers holding unredeemed gift vouchers most at risk.
Gift cards may be ‘worthless’ soon Angus Kidman, from consumer comparison site Finder, said customers with David Jones gift cards should use them as soon as possible.
“If the business doesn’t find a buyer, that gift card will almost certainly be worthless,” Kidman said.
“Stores appear to be accepting gift cards for now, so don’t delay. That also applies to any discounts you’ve earned through David Jones Rewards.”

The collapse marks the first time David Jones has been in administration, having previously weathered nearly two centuries while cycling through almost every type of ownership model, from public listing to foreign conglomerate ownership and, most recently, private equity.
Anchorage Capital Partners, which bought David Jones from South Africa’s Woolworths in 2023, has now lost operational control after failing to turn the struggling retailer around.
The retailer’s main landlord, Scentre, said on Wednesday that David Jones had not paid rent since September.

“We have made a generous offer to Anchorage Capital that would have facilitated the continuation of David Jones trading and that offer has disappointingly been rejected by them,” Scentre said in a statement.

excerpt_en: Other lives: Academic in the field of special educational needs with a passion for lifelong learning in heritage and the arts
body_en: Nick Peacey, who has died aged 83, was known in north London for his work with Lauderdale House, the arts and education centre in a rescued Tudor building in Highgate. He combined a commitment to improving educational opportunities with a passion for local history and the arts.

Born in Salisbury, Wiltshire, to Theodosia (nee Hale), a social worker, and Thomas Peacey, who ran a bookshop, Nick went to Lancing college in West Sussex, and then studied classics at Christ Church, Oxford, from 1961.

He spent most of his professional career working in the field of special educational needs and disability (Send), teaching in the London borough of Haringey, where he supported young people excluded – or at the risk of exclusion – from school. He joined the UCL Institute of Education in 1990, where he worked with local and national government and international organisations on Send development and teacher education.

Alongside his career, Nick devoted almost 50 years to Lauderdale House, which I joined in 1998, becoming director in 2013. He became a founding trustee of the Lauderdale House Society in 1978 and served as chair from 1983 until 2017, helping transform the fire-damaged historic building into the thriving independent arts and heritage charity it is today. Following the completion of its £2.1m restoration he was appointed MBE in 2018. He continued as vice-chair until his death.

An advocate for heritage and learning, he also led the campaign from 2018 to return the Highgate Roman kiln – excavated in the 1960s and 70s but later in pieces in storage at the Bruce Castle museum in Tottenham – to its original site in Highgate Wood, securing funding from the National Heritage Lottery Fund for its restoration and public interpretation. As a young teacher in the early 70s, he had been involved in a project to build several reconstructions of the kiln and to undertake experimental firing of vessels.

He also founded the Gallipoli Music Memorial charity, marking the centenary of the Gallipoli campaign through music, education and remembrance, inspired by the story of his great-uncle the composer William Denis Browne, killed in action in June 1915.

Nick’s interests were remarkably wide-ranging. He was a board member of the charity Foundation Years Information and Research, formed by professionals, academics and policy makers interested in the field of child development, and chaired by MPs, originally Frank Field, and subsequently Catherine West and Maya Ellis; the group seeks to promote understanding of the extent to which earliest relationships shape a baby’s brain and to highlight the importance of resources and structures to support caregivers.

He was also a fellow of the UCL Institute of Education Centre for Educational Inclusion and an active Labour party supporter, and he researched his own family history, publishing in 2013 The Inflations & Deflations of the Spencer Family: Balloons, Bikes & Camels.
In 1968 he married Lindy Hill. She survives him, along with their two daughters, Sarah and Caroline, and two grandchildren.

excerpt_en: Other lives: Entomologist who found ways to deal with insects that attack tropical cash crops such as cocoa and coffee
body_en: My father, Mike Bigger, who has died aged 95, was an expert on insect pests of tropical cash crops, particularly cocoa, coffee, cashew, teak and eucalyptus.

Employed by the Overseas Development Agency as a tropical entomologist from the late 1950s until the early 90s, he lived all over the world, establishing research stations in Tanzania, Kenya, Ghana, the Solomon Islands and Bhutan and becoming an early adopter of the mathematical modelling of insect populations, which enabled him to propose alternatives to blanket pesticide spraying of tropical cash crops.

He discovered, for example, that changing the density of trees used to shade cocoa plantations can help to promote black or weaver ants that drive out smaller fire ants, whose stings can result in severe burns for cocoa plantation workers.

Mike was born to British parents in Nablus, in what was then the British Mandate of Palestine (now the West Bank), where his father, William, was a medical doctor and his mother, Dorothy (nee Vigers), was a pharmacist.

When Palestine began to descend into violence, the family moved to the UK, where Mike was educated at Campbell college, Belfast. He subsequently studied natural sciences at Trinity College Dublin and tropical entomology at the Imperial College of Tropical Agriculture in Trinidad (1955-56).

On his return to the UK, he joined the Overseas Development Agency, which in 1957 sent him on his first foreign posting, to Nachingwea in Tanganyika (now Tanzania). While on leave, he met Gerry Whitcroft, a biologist; they married in 1962 and spent much of the rest of their life together living in far-flung locations. Often they lived for long periods with few visitors and only a short-wave radio for communication, but they thoroughly enjoyed their experiences over the years.

After a final posting for Mike in Bhutan, from 1989 they lived in happy retirement in Herefordshire. He donated his insect collections to various institutions, including the British Museum; sadly many that he left behind in the Solomon Islands were destroyed during a coup there in 2000.

As well as being an intellectually rigorous scientist, Mike was extremely creative, and his drawings of insects were published in seven books, including The Insect Pests of Forest Plantation Trees in the Solomon Islands (1988) and A Guide to Insect Pests of Nigerian Crops (1996). He was also a master wood carver, and made tapestries and wooden toys.
Gerry died in 2024. Mike is survived by their two children, Clare and me, and five grandchildren.

title_en: Donald Trump’s Republicans suffer landslide defeat – what this means for the world
excerpt_en: Facing a hostile Congress, the US president is likely to focus on foreign policy to secure his legacy.
body_en: Donald Trump’s Republican Party has received a stunning rebuke in the US midterm elections. Republicans went into the evening hoping that the polls might be wrong and that they could at least cling on to control of the Senate. But by midnight in Washington, the GOP was staring down what looked like its worst defeat in 50 years.

Republican losses were not just confined to the type of swing districts that parties usually worry about on election night. The scale of the losses was staggering. They lost Senate seats in deep red states such as Texas and South Carolina. They lost districts they had gerrymandered and in which they were supposed to be unbeatable. They lost seats that even the sharpest analysts thought were safe.

Why? For months, surveys have shown that voters are fed up with high prices, with the war in Iran, and with what is increasingly being talked about as the Trump administration’s corruption. A president who was narrowly elected on the promise of a steady economic hand instead spent two years pursuing an extreme ideological agenda favoured only by a minority of Americans. He ignored what voters were saying, and now they have delivered a harsh verdict.
Read more: What recent polling suggests will happen in the US midterm elections

But these results have implications beyond just the remainder of Trump’s presidency. They break some of the patterns that have defined American politics for decades. Democrats are suddenly winning in places where they have been counted out for a generation. Suddenly, the American political map looks different.

Take Texas. The last time a Democrat won election as a senator there was 1988. Democrats have not won a presidential election in Texas since Jimmy Carter in 1976. Yet last night, Democrat James Talarico powered to a convincing victory. If elections in Texas become politically competitive on a permanent basis, it will become much harder for Republicans to take the presidency in the future.

The Republican Party will now be looking nervously towards the 2028 election. For the first time since 2016, there is likely to be a serious debate within the party about whether to move on from the aggressive nationalism and bigotry of Trump’s “Make America Great Again” movement. Democrats, meanwhile, face their own questions about how to capitalise on their victories.

Foreign policy futures But for the rest of the world, change might not come so quickly. Despite the fact that his party has suffered this electoral setback, Trump remains president until 2028. And because despite its constitutional role in declaring war and ratifying treaties, Congress tends to be less involved in foreign policy, there is still a lot that he can do with that power.

Indeed, US presidents whose parties perform badly in midterm elections often become more active in foreign policy than they had previously. With the chance of passing a significant domestic agenda mostly beyond their reach, they have a more time on their hands to think about America’s relations with the rest of the world. The same is likely to be true of Trump.

The fact that the midterms are over also means that Trump no longer has to be so careful about the political consequences of his actions. As the midterm elections got closer, the president has backed down from major military confrontation with Iran and sought a truce in his tariff wars. Now, with political constraints lifted, he could become more erratic and unpredictable.

Congress would not be completely powerless to stop him, at least in theory. But most actions it can take – such as cutting off funding for the war with Iran or seizing tariff power back from the president – require margins of control in both chambers that Democrats are unlikely to have, despite their formidable victories.

They would need to have a two-thirds majority to override an almost certain presidential veto on any attempt to pass laws to achieve these outcomes. So a key question is whether this midterm drubbing was serious enough to make some Republican members of Congress get serious about joining Democrats in restraining Trump.

Something that Democrats will definitely be able to do is launch all manner of investigations into the conduct of the Trump administration and some of its officials. Their efforts are likely to focus on the war with Iran, Trump’s personal financial dealings with foreign leaders, and the management of the Pentagon by secretary of defence Pete Hegseth.
Hegseth, indeed, could be an early casualty of these efforts – there is speculation that he will resign or be fired rather than face possible impeachment.

But ultimately a change of direction in US foreign policy depends on the decisions of Trump himself. A changing of the guard among his advisers, or in Congress, can only do so much to influence a president who has never willingly submitted to constraint.
The world should prepare itself for the possibility that a politically wounded and angry Trump could now decide to vent his frustrations abroad.
Andrew Gawthorpe is a senior fellow at the Foreign Policy Centre in London.

title_en: ‘Epic’ blue wave helps Democrats take Congress in overwhelming rebuke to President Trump
excerpt_en: Election Day turned into a massive rebuke of President Donald Trump: a blue wave not seen in 20 years that was built on transforming the economy and rising prices into a central line of attack.
body_en: Supporters of South Carolina Democratic Senate candidate Annie Andrews cheer during her election night watch party on Nov. 3, 2026, in Charleston, S.C. AP Photo/Mic Smith Voters turned out in massive numbers on Election Day to hand Democrats control of Congress, in a sweeping snub of President Donald Trump and Republicans. Democrats won several statewide races in places long considered GOP bastions, including races that were considered insurmountable even weeks ago.

Democrats took control of the House and Senate, flipping Senate seats in Texas, South Carolina, North Carolina, Kansas and Ohio. The results reflected broad dissatisfaction across the country with Trump, his agenda and the candidates he had endorsed.
The Conversation’s senior politics editor, Alfonso Serrano, spoke on election night with Charlie Hunt, a scholar at Boise State University who studies Congress and elections.

It was obviously a strong showing for Democrats on Election Day, something that was even evident in the margin of some Democratic losses. What does it tell you, for example, that democratic socialist Angie Nixon fought a competitive race for the Senate in Florida?

There is this big uniform shift toward the Democrats that we’re seeing really across virtually all kinds of locations and geographies and counties. What I think is particularly notable here, and something we were on the lookout for in this election, and we’re seeing it, is the substantial shift in the Hispanic vote from 2024 in places like Texas and Florida, where you’re getting these 30-to-35 point shifts from how Donald Trump performed in 2024. That was a big part of what helped him win, and it seems like it has snapped right back and even farther in the other direction. This is what made Florida, I think, closer than a lot of folks thought.

It’s what put a number of really, really right-leaning districts in play, particularly in South Florida. And it looks like it is going to help Democrats keep the number of seats they had in Florida in the House that they had before the election, which is incredible when you consider that Florida did this mid-decade gerrymander to try to get them out of a bunch of those seats.

Some rural areas of the country were also more competitive than expected, like North Carolina’s 11th Congressional District, where Democrat Jaime Ager flipped a conservative district. What does that tell you?

It’s definitely an indicator of at least one of these two things. One is just really massive Democratic turnout across the board. Regardless of where they live, Democrats were so enthusiastic and energized to turn out that they did so across all different types of districts and counties.

It could also be an indicator of some cross-party voting, where Republicans are crossing over in some cases and voting for the Democrat. I don’t imagine there’s a ton of that, but in a lot of these close districts, and if you’ve got enough of those folks in places like Texas, it really does make a big difference, those small shifts.

I think we’re probably also likely to see, and we saw some of this in the exit polling, a major shift in independent voters, unaffiliated voters, toward the Democrats, whereas in 2024 they had been closer to Trump.

Voter numbers in some key areas were at levels typically seen only in presidential election years. That surge in turnout helps explain why Democrats outperformed expectations in the midterm elections,according to political scientist Charlie Hunt. I’d like to go back to turnout briefly. Turnout looks like it was strong across the country. In Georgia, for example, Election Day’s turnout was on pace to beat turnout in the 2024 presidential elections.

That’s unprecedented, at least in modern elections. In Texas, for example, in some counties we saw James Talarico getting as many raw votes as Kamala Harris did in a presidential election. This isn’t a very political science term, but that’s insane. In a midterm election you typically see 10% or 15% less turnout than you would in a presidential election. But Democrats voted in presidential-level numbers in a lot of these really key areas, and that’s explaining how they’re able to overperform at levels we haven’t seen in at least 20 years.

Voters cast their ballots on Election Day at the Cross Insurance Center polling location on Nov. 3, 2026, in Bangor, Maine. Joe Raedle/Getty Images Elon Musk spent nearly half a billion dollars supporting Republican candidates, including some US$200 million in Texas to elect Ken Paxton for the Senate, who lost. What does that tell you about the influence of political spending?

Republican PACs, super PACs and billionaire donors like Elon Musk may have raised more money compared to Democrats, but Democratic candidates themselves outraised Republican candidates through donors that gave directly to their campaigns.

This is important for a couple of reasons. Number one, because candidates get much better rates on TV ad buys than outside spenders. And so they get more bang for their buck when they’re spending on advertisements, which is the most expensive component of any campaign. And more to the point, that is an indicator of sort of dedicated grassroots donors who turn into voters, whereas Musk gets one vote at the end of the day.

And there is no amount of money that can make up for a really flawed candidate like Ken Paxton. And more to the point, a lot of this money, once you get into the tens, the hundreds of millions of dollars, a lot of the research talks about the diminishing returns that you get on that. Going from zero dollars spent to $10 million spent, that’s a very different kind of campaign. But once you go from $500 million to $510 million, that’s not going to get you a whole lot more votes.
